Coast mole (Scapanus orarius) neonates are altricial at birth, weighing approximately 5 grams [Wwb = approximately 5 grams], a value estimated from measurements of the closely related Townsend's mole. This modest birth mass reflects the substantial energetic investment required during a gestation period that lasts approximately 28 days [tg = approximately 28 days] when the female maintains a core body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. During this time, the gestating embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis within the uterine environment, ultimately emerging as a pink, hairless pup entirely dependent on maternal care. The suckling juvenile phase is characterized by intensive nursing, and the nutritional dependence on milk continues until the offspring achieves a wet weight of roughly 40 grams [Wwx = roughly 40 grams] at weaning. This entire weaning process, from birth to the cessation of lactation, spans approximately 40 days after birth [tx = approximately 40 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 35 °C, after which the weaned juvenile begins consuming soil invertebrates at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] independently.

Under a stable core temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], as the juvenile transitions into a sub-adult, it undergoes a period of rapid somatic growth, ultimately reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 85 grams [Wwi = about 85 grams], though published accounts from the Animal Diversity Web suggest a typical range between 61 and 91 grams for fully grown adults. This asymptotic mass is achieved well before the onset of sexual maturity, which is estimated to occur at roughly 300 days after birth [tp = roughly 300 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The attainment of puberty marks a significant physiological milestone, at which point the reproductive tract becomes fully functional and the individual is capable of participating in the annual breeding cycle. The duration of this pre-reproductive period likely reflects the time necessary for the skeletal and muscular systems to reach adequate size for successful burrowing and foraging in the competitive subterranean environment.

Reproductive output in the Coast mole is constrained by a relatively low annual fecundity. Females typically produce 3 to 4 litters each year [F_R_i = 3 to 4 litters each year], with each litter containing between 3 and 4 pups [N_R_i = each litter containing between 3 and 4 pups], a pattern consistent with the slow life-history strategy common among talpid moles. This annual reproductive rate is observed under typical physiological conditions when the female's body temperature is maintained near 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. The combination of a modest litter size and a single annual reproductive event results in a limited annual recruitment, underscoring the species' reliance on high offspring survival rather than high fecundity. The timing of parturition is likely synchronized with peak spring invertebrate abundance, ensuring that the lactating female can meet the elevated energetic costs of milk production while the neonates have access to sufficient prey upon weaning.

Basal metabolic rate measurements provide insight into the energetic demands that underpin this life history. Respirometry trials conducted at a body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] have recorded a resting oxygen consumption of 64.1 milliliters per hour [JOi = 64.1 milliliters per hour], representing the maximum basal metabolic rate for the species. This relatively high metabolic rate, characteristic of insectivorous mammals that must sustain intense foraging activity in low-oxygen burrow systems, necessitates a correspondingly high food intake rate. The energetic costs of thermoregulation at the species' preferred body temperature are substantial, and the mole's daily energy budget must accommodate not only basal maintenance but also the considerable muscular effort required for tunnel excavation. Field observations suggest that individuals may consume invertebrates equivalent to their own body mass daily to meet these metabolic demands, particularly during the energetically demanding breeding season.

Maximum longevity records for the Coast mole remain somewhat speculative, but available data suggest a lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under natural conditions when body temperature is maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, common among small-bodied insectivorous mammals, constrains the total number of reproductive events an individual can achieve across its lifetime. Given the single annual litter and the four-year maximum longevity, a female may produce only four litters in her lifetime, yielding a total of 12 to 16 pups. Such a low lifetime reproductive output places a premium on adult survival between breeding seasons and highlights the importance of secure burrow systems that provide protection from predators and environmental extremes. Senescence in older individuals is characterized by declining foraging efficiency and gradual loss of body condition, ultimately leading to natural mortality.
